Conversation notes · English

Small details, useful distinctions

Two small checks for your next conversation

When you talk about time or describe a place, these two quick checks can help. Explore either one, or just take the reminders with you.

A light-touch review The supplied notes contain one correction for each point, in separate sessions. Neither is established as a recurring pattern.
01

Time: length or starting point?

Before choosing for or since, ask: “How long—or from when?”

for + a length of time

since + a starting point

From your conversation

Original

I have lived here since three years.

Correction

I have lived here for three years.

“Three years” tells us the length of time, not when it began. Keep “I have lived”; change only the time word.

02

There is—or there are?

After there, look ahead: “Am I talking about one thing or more than one?”

There is + a singular noun phrase

There are + a plural noun phrase

From your conversation

Original

There is two small parks nearby.

Correction

There are two small parks nearby.

“Two small parks” is plural, so use “are” in standard English. This is a useful default for careful speech and writing.

Take one check into your next conversation

Talking about how long you have lived somewhere? Think length → for. Describing what is nearby? Think plural → there are. You do not need to monitor everything at once.
